young.html: Niccolò Machiavelli worked for the city of Florence, in Italy, about five hundred years ago, as a kind of messenger and adviser who traveled to meet kings and generals. When the rulers of Florence changed, he lost his job. At home on his little farm, he wrote a short book called The Prince, full of advice for anyone who rules a country.

Most advice books of his time told rulers to be good, kind and honest. Machiavelli said: let us look at how rulers really act, and what really works. Some of his advice is wise, like getting ready for trouble before it comes. Some of it shocked people then and still does, like saying a ruler sometimes has to break his promises.

young.name: gb-fortune-river
young.cap: Machiavelli's picture: luck is like a river that floods. Build the dikes while the weather is calm.

young.html: Because of this book, people today call a sneaky, scheming person "Machiavellian." Whether that is fair to Machiavelli is one of the questions grown-ups still argue about.

Feared or loved? Machiavelli asks whether it is better for a leader to be loved or feared. Think of a good team captain, teacher or coach. Do people follow them because they like them, because they respect them, or because they are a little afraid of them? Make two lists, then talk about it: is there a third answer Machiavelli missed?
young.title: Talk it over

full.html: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) served the Republic of Florence for fourteen years as a secretary and diplomat, and met the hard men of his age, above all Cesare Borgia. In 1512 the Medici family returned to power, the republic fell, and Machiavelli was dismissed, briefly jailed and questioned under torture, then released. In 1513, living on his farm outside the city, he wrote The Prince and dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici, hoping for work. It was printed only in 1532, after his death.

Machiavelli's great move, in Chapter XV, is to say he will write about the real truth of things, how people actually live, rather than imagined ideal states. A prince who always tries to be good among so many who are not, he says, will come to ruin. So the prince must learn how to do wrong, and use that knowledge or not as necessity requires.

full.name: gb-principalities
full.cap: The book begins with a map of kinds of state. Tap each to see what Machiavelli says about it.

full.text: Upon this a question arises: whether it be better to be loved than feared or feared than loved? It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
full.author: Machiavelli

full.html: Read the whole chapter, though, and the picture is more careful. A prince must above all avoid being hated, and the surest way to be hated, he says, is to take people's property. Fear without hatred keeps a state stable; cruelty that breeds hatred destroys it.

full.text: A prince, therefore, being compelled knowingly to adopt the beast, ought to choose the fox and the lion; because the lion cannot defend himself against snares and the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. Therefore, it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves.
full.author: Machiavelli

full.html: In the same chapter he says a prince need not keep his word when keeping it would harm him, but must seem merciful, faithful, humane, upright and religious. This is the advice that made his name a byword for deceit.

Two words run through the book. Fortuna is chance, the turns of events no one controls. Virtù is not quite our "virtue": it is a ruler's skill, energy and nerve. In Chapter XXV he says that "Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions," leaving the other half, or a little less, to us, and compares her to a river in flood that does its worst where no dikes were built in calm weather.

full.title: Machiavelli's argument, laid out
full.q: Chapter XVII: why is it safer to be feared than loved?
steps: Premise: people are, in general, ungrateful and self-interested.
Premise: love is a bond of obligation, which people break when it suits them.
Premise: fear is kept up by the dread of punishment, which never fails.
Conclusion: so, if a prince must choose, being feared is safer, provided he is not hated.
full.a: The conclusion rests on a claim about human nature. To argue with Machiavelli, you can question that first premise.

head: Reading
The case for it
The case against it
rows: It openly advises cruelty and deceit "when necessary"; the Church banned it in 1559, and "Machiavellian" became a word for scheming.
It also insists on avoiding hatred, on laws and good arms, and on the common good of Italy.
Rousseau and others thought it exposed how tyrants work, so that free people could see it.
Machiavelli seems sincere in seeking a post from the Medici.
It studies power as it is, as later realists did.
Critics say it separates politics from morality too sharply.
full.cap: Three main readings (our summary). Scholars still debate them.

full.html: Machiavelli's longer Discourses on Livy, written about the same time, praises free republics where citizens share power, and many readers think it shows his deeper loyalties. The two books are best read together.

Assuming Machiavelli said "the end justifies the means." That phrase is not in The Prince. He did argue that a ruler will be judged by results, which is close, and readers disagree about how far he meant it.

deep.html: In Machiavelli's day Italy was divided into rival states, Florence, Venice, Milan, Naples and the Papal States among them, while France and Spain sent armies through it. The last chapter of The Prince is a passionate plea for a leader to unite Italy and drive the "barbarians" out. Some readers see the whole book as written toward that hope.

items: Should leaders be judged by the same rules as everyone else, or are there times when a ruler must do what an ordinary person should not?
Is Machiavelli right that people are mostly self-interested? What evidence would count for or against him?
Can fear keep order without becoming hatred? Where is the line?
How much of life is fortune, and how much is up to us?

deep.html: Later books on this ladder answer him: Hobbes builds on a dark view of human nature; Locke, Montesquieu and the authors of the Federalist look for ways to limit rulers through laws and checks. Shakespeare's history plays, also in this era, show kings who live and die by Machiavelli's rules.

questions: Is it better for a leader to be loved or feared? Can someone be both?
Machiavelli says a ruler must sometimes break a promise. Is that ever right? Can you think of a case on each side?
What "dikes" could you build now, in calm weather, against future trouble?
Why do you think Machiavelli's name became a word for scheming? Is that fair?
Should we judge an author by his worst advice or by his whole book?
care: Machiavelli writes frankly about cruelty, deceit and war as tools of power. This lesson presents his arguments as his views, with the main criticisms, and quotes nothing graphic.
